summary: Specifies Manufacturer Usage Descriptions, an architecture that lets end devices signal to the network what access and functionality they need. The initial focus is access control.

plainLanguage.summary: A light bulb only ever needs to talk to one service. This document lets a device say so: it gives the network an address of a signed file listing the traffic it is meant to have, and the network blocks the rest. The local administrator decides how much of that advice to take.

questions: how does mud url work with dhcp
subtitle: How a device can point the network to a signed file saying what traffic it is meant to send and receive.

tldr.problem: Devices built for one narrow purpose, such as a light bulb, only need a few communication patterns, but networks have no standard way to learn what those are and block everything else.
tldr.mechanism: The device emits a MUD URL, by DHCP, an X.509 certificate extension or LLDP. A MUD manager fetches the signed MUD file from that https URL, a YANG-based JSON access list, and turns it into local network configuration.
tldr.outcome: MUD gives a way to scale access policy across many device types, but the file is a suggestion that the local administrator can ignore, and it does not replace patching.

facts.label: cache-validity limit
facts.value: At most 168 hours; at least 24 recommended

today: RFC 8520 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the access list model of RFC 8519.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet has largely been constructed for general purpose computers, those devices that may be used for a purpose specified by those who own the device. In the original reasoning it was presumed that an end device would be most capable of protecting itself. That made sense when the typical device was a workstation or a mainframe, and it continues to make sense for general purpose computing devices today, including laptops, smart phones and tablets.

Consider instead a group of objects that are specifically not intended to be used for general purpose computing tasks. These devices, which the document calls Things, have a specific purpose, and by definition all other uses are not intended. If a small number of communication patterns follows from those small number of uses, the combination of these two statements can be restated as a Manufacturer Usage Description that can be applied at various points within a network. MUD primarily addresses threats to the device rather than the device as a threat. In some circumstances, however, MUD may offer some protection in the latter case, depending on how the MUD URL is communicated and how devices and their communications are authenticated.

The term 'manufacturer' is used loosely to refer to the entity or organisation that will state how a device is intended to be used. In the context of a light bulb this might indeed be the manufacturer; in the context of a smarter device with a built-in Linux stack it might be an integrator. The key points are that the device is assumed to serve a limited purpose, and that there exists an organisation in the supply chain of that device which will take responsibility for informing the network about that purpose.

The intent of MUD is to substantially reduce the threat surface on a device to those communications intended by the manufacturer, to provide a means to scale network policies to the ever-increasing number of types of devices in the network, to provide a means to address at least some vulnerabilities in a way that is faster than the time it might take to update systems, to keep the cost of implementation to the bare minimum, and to provide a means of extensibility for manufacturers to express other device capabilities or requirements.

MUD consists of three architectural building blocks: a URL that can be used to locate a description, the description itself including how it is interpreted, and a means for local network management systems to retrieve the description. MUD is most effective when the network is able to identify in some way the remote endpoints that Things will talk to.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices have one job and one set of conversations. This document lets the maker of such a device tell the network what those are, so the network can refuse everything else.

sections.title: What MUD Does Not Do
sections.content:
MUD is not intended to address network authorization of general purpose computers, as their manufacturers cannot envision a specific communication pattern to describe. In addition, even those devices that have a single or small number of uses might have very broad communication patterns, and MUD on its own is not for them either.

Although MUD can provide network administrators with some additional protection when device vulnerabilities exist, it will never replace the need for manufacturers to patch vulnerabilities. Finally, no matter what the manufacturer specifies in a MUD file, these are not directives but suggestions. How they are instantiated locally will depend on many factors and will be ultimately up to the local network administrator, who must decide what is appropriate in a given circumstance.

The example the document gives is a light bulb that is intended to light a room. It may be remotely controlled through the network, and it may make use of a rendezvous service which could be accessed by an application on a smart phone. All other network access is unwanted: it will not contact a news service, nor speak to the refrigerator, and it has no need of a printer or other devices. Applying an access list that states it will only connect to the single rendezvous service will not impede performing its function, and at the same time gives the device an additional layer of protection.
sections.plainLanguage: MUD is a suggestion, not an order. The local administrator can ignore it, and it never replaces fixing the bugs in the device.

sections.title: The MUD Architecture
sections.content:
When the MUD URL is resolved, the MUD manager retrieves a file that describes what sort of communications a device is designed to have. The manufacturer may specify either specific hosts for cloud-based services or certain classes for access within an operational network. An example of a class might be 'devices of a specified manufacturer type', where the manufacturer type is indicated by the authority component of the MUD URL. Another might be to allow or disallow local access. Just like other policies, these may be combined, for example to allow access to devices of the same manufacturer, to allow access to and from controllers via the Constrained Application Protocol, to allow access to local DNS and NTP, and to deny all other access.

The files that are retrieved are intended to be closely aligned to existing network architectures so that they are easy to deploy. YANG is used because it provides accurate and adequate models for use by network devices, and JSON is used as a serialization format for compactness and readability relative to XML. Other formats may be chosen with later versions of MUD. While the policy examples focus on access control, this is not intended to be the sole focus: by structuring the model with clear extension points, other descriptions such as quality of service could be included.

The YANG modules specified are extensions of the access control list model of RFC 8519. One module specifies a means for domain names to be used in access control lists, so that devices that have their controllers in the cloud may be appropriately authorized with domain names, where the mapping of those names to addresses may rapidly change. The other module abstracts away IP addresses into certain classes that are instantiated into actual IP addresses through local processing. The abstractions map to zero or more hosts as follows: manufacturer, a device made by a particular manufacturer as identified by the authority component of its MUD URL; same-manufacturer, devices that have the same authority component of their MUD URL; controller, devices that the local network administrator admits to the particular class; my-controller, devices intended to serve as controllers for the MUD URL that the Thing emitted; and local, the class of IP addresses scoped within some administrative boundary, by default the local subnet.

In the architecture, the switch or router collects MUD URLs and forwards them to the MUD manager, a network management system, for processing. This happens in different ways depending on how the URL is communicated: in the case of DHCP the DHCP server might receive the URL and then process it, and in the case of IEEE 802.1X the switch would carry the URL via a certificate to the authentication server via EAP over RADIUS, which would then process it.

The information returned by the MUD file server is valid for as long as the Thing is connected, with no expiry, though if the MUD manager detects that the MUD file for a Thing has changed it SHOULD update the policy expeditiously. The web server is typically run by or on behalf of the manufacturer, and its domain name is that of the authority found in the MUD URL. For legacy cases where Things cannot emit a URL, the switch may proxy it, for example by hardcoding a MUD URL on a switch port or mapping an available identifier such as an L2 address or certificate hash to a MUD URL.

The role of the MUD manager is to receive MUD URLs, fetch MUD files, translate abstractions in the MUD files to specific network element configuration, maintain and update any required mappings of the abstractions, and update network elements with appropriate configuration. A MUD manager may be a component of an AAA system or a network management system.
sections.plainLanguage: The device's maker hosts a file on the web describing what the device needs. The network's management system fetches that file, works out which addresses it means for this particular network, and programs the switch with an access list.

sections.title: The MUD Model
sections.content:
A MUD file consists of a YANG model instance that has been serialized in JSON. For the purposes of MUD, the nodes that can be modified are access lists as augmented by this model. The MUD file is limited to the serialization of only three YANG schemas: the access control list model of RFC 8519, the ietf-mud module defined by this document, and the ietf-acldns module also defined by this document.

The root container is mud. It holds the MUD version, the MUD URL, the date and time at which the file was generated, the location of the signature, the cache validity, a flag saying whether the device supports MUD, system information such as the manufacturer name, model name, firmware revision and software revision, a documentation URL, and a list of extensions. It also holds two containers, to-device-policy and from-device-policy, each of which holds access lists for traffic towards the device and away from it.

The cache-validity leaf is a uint8 giving the period in hours that a network management station MUST wait since its last retrieval before checking for an update. It is RECOMMENDED that this value be no less than 24, and it MUST NOT be more than 168 for any Thing that is supported. The period SHOULD be no shorter than any period determined through HTTP caching directives. Expiry of this timer does not require the MUD manager to discard the MUD file, nor to terminate access to a Thing.
sections.plainLanguage: The file itself is a small JSON document: a version number, the address of the file, when it was made, how long it stays valid, and two lists of access rules, one for traffic going to the device and one for traffic coming from it.

sections.title: Communicating the MUD URL
sections.content:
MUD URLs MUST use the 'https' scheme, in order to establish the MUD file server's identity and assure the integrity of the MUD file. Any 'https://' URL can be a MUD URL, and a manufacturer may construct one in any way. Three means of emitting the MUD URL are defined in the document.

The first is a DHCP option that the DHCP client uses to inform the DHCP server. The IPv4 option has code OPTION_MUD_URL_V4, 161, with a one-octet length followed by the MUD string. The MUD string is the MUD URL, optionally followed by a space and a reserved string that will be defined in future specifications; MUD managers that do not understand that field MUST ignore it. The entire option MUST NOT exceed 255 octets. The IPv6 option has code OPTION_MUD_URL_V6, 112, with an option length followed by the MUD string. A DHCPv4 client MAY emit a DHCPv4 option and a DHCPv6 client MAY emit a DHCPv6 option; because clients are intended to have at most one MUD URL associated with them they may emit at most one MUD URL option via DHCPv4 and one via DHCPv6, and where both are emitted the same URL MUST be used. A DHCP server may ignore the options or act on them, either forwarding the URL and client information to a network management system or retrieving the usage description itself.

The second is an X.509 extension. IEEE 802.1AR provides a certificate-based approach to communicate device characteristics, and the MUD URL extension is non-critical, as required by that standard. The extension contains a single URL pointing to an online Manufacturer Usage Description concerning the certificate subject, and the URI must be represented as described in Section 7.4 of RFC 5280. A separate new extension is defined as id-pe-mudsigner, which contains the subject field of the signing certificate of the MUD file.

The third is a Link Layer Discovery Protocol frame. LLDP is a one-hop, vendor-neutral link-layer protocol used by Things for advertising their identity, capabilities and neighbours on an IEEE 802 local area network, and its Type-Length-Value design allows vendor-specific extensions. The MUD LLDP extension uses a vendor-specific frame with TLV Type 127, a 9-bit length field, the IANA organizationally unique identifier 00 00 5E, subtype 1, and a MUD string of 1 to 255 octets whose length MUST NOT exceed 255 octets. Hosts, routers or other network elements that implement this option are intended to have at most one MUD URL associated with them, so they may transmit at most one MUD URL value.
sections.plainLanguage: The URL travels in one of three ways: as an option in the address request, as a field in the device's certificate, or as an extra field in the neighbour announcement the device sends on the link. In all three cases it is just an https address.

sections.title: Signed MUD Files
sections.content:
Because MUD files contain information that may be used to configure network access lists, they are sensitive. To ensure that they have not been tampered with, it is important that they be signed. DER-encoded Cryptographic Message Syntax is used for this purpose.

A MUD file MUST be signed using CMS as an opaque binary object. In order to make successful verification more likely, intermediate certificates SHOULD be included. The signature is stored at the location specified in the MUD file, and signatures are transferred using the content type 'application/pkcs7-signature'. A MUD file may need to be re-signed if the signature expires.

Prior to processing the rest of a MUD file, the MUD manager MUST retrieve the MUD signature file by retrieving the value of the 'mud-signature' entry and validating the signature across the MUD file. The Key Usage Extension in the signing certificate MUST be present and have the digitalSignature bit set. When the id-pe-mudsigner extension is present in a device's X.509 certificate, the MUD signature file MUST have been generated by a certificate whose subject matches the contents of that extension. If these conditions are not met, or if the chain of trust cannot be validated to a known trust anchor, the MUD manager MUST cease processing the MUD file until an administrator has given approval.

The purpose of the signature on the file is to assign accountability to an entity, whose reputation can be used to guide administrators on whether to accept a given MUD file. While it is likely that the manufacturer will be the signer of the file, this is not strictly necessary and may not be desirable: integrators may install their own certificates, and what matters more is the accountability of the recommendation rather than only the relationship between the Thing and the file.
sections.plainLanguage: The file must be signed, and the signature is checked against a trusted certificate before any of the file is used. If the check fails, the file is not applied until an administrator approves it.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Because MUD consists of a number of architectural building blocks, it is possible to assemble different deployment scenarios. One key aspect is where to place policy enforcement. In order to protect the Thing from other Things within a local deployment, policy can be enforced on the nearest switch or access point. In order to limit unwanted traffic within a network, it may also be advisable to enforce policy as close to the Internet as possible. In some circumstances policy enforcement may not be available at the closest hop, and at that point the risk of lateral infection, that is, infection of devices that reside near one another, is increased to the number of Things that are able to communicate without protection.

A caution about some of the classes: admission of a Thing into the 'manufacturer' and 'same-manufacturer' class may have an impact on the access of other Things. The administrator has to weigh the benefit of a policy that is easier to write against the risk that admitting one device widens the access of others.
sections.plainLanguage: Where the rules are enforced is a choice: next to the device, to protect it from its neighbours, or near the edge of the network, to keep traffic inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Based on how a MUD URL is emitted, a Thing may be able to lie about what it is and so gain additional network access. This can happen when a device emits a MUD URL using DHCP or LLDP, such as being inappropriately admitted to a class such as 'same-manufacturer', being given access to a device such as 'my-controller', or being permitted access to an Internet resource where that access would otherwise be disallowed. Implementations SHOULD be configurable to disallow additive access for devices using MUD URLs that are not emitted in a secure fashion such as in a certificate, and SHOULD NOT grant elevated permissions to devices that do not strongly bind their identity to their L2 and L3 transmissions.

Devices may forge source information, so deployments should apply appropriate protections to bind communications to the authentication that has taken place. For 802.1X authentication, IEEE 802.1AE (MACsec) is one means by which this may happen, and a similar approach can be used with 802.11i. Implementations using session-oriented access that is not cryptographically bound should take care to remove state when any form of break in the session is detected.

A rogue certification authority may sign a certificate containing the same subject name as the MUDsigner field in the manufacturer certificate, thus seemingly permitting a substitute MUD file for a device. There are two mitigations: if the signer changes this may be flagged as an exception by the MUD manager, and if the MUD file also changes the MUD manager SHOULD seek administrator approval. In all circumstances the MUD manager MUST maintain a cache of trusted CAs for this purpose, and when such a rogue is discovered it SHOULD be removed.

When certificates are not present, Things claiming to be of a certain manufacturer SHOULD NOT be included in that manufacturer grouping without additional validation. MUD managers SHOULD NOT accept a usage description for a Thing with the same MAC address that has indicated a change of the URL authority without some additional validation, and new Things that present some form of unauthenticated MUD URL SHOULD be validated by some external means when they would be given increased network access.

It may be possible for a rogue manufacturer to inappropriately exercise the MUD file parser in order to exploit a vulnerability. Two approaches are recommended: validate that the signer of the MUD file is known to and trusted by the MUD manager, and have a system do a primary scan of the file to ensure that it is both parseable and believable at some level. It may also be useful to limit retrieval of MUD URLs to only those sites that are known to have decent web or domain reputations. Use of a URL necessitates the use of domain names, so if a domain name changes ownership the new owner may be able to provide MUD files that MUD managers would consider valid; MUD managers SHOULD cache the certificates used by the MUD file server and check whether ownership of the domain has changed.

The release of a MUD URL by a Thing reveals what the Thing is and provides an attacker with guidance on what vulnerabilities may be present. While the MUD URL itself is not intended to be unique to a specific Thing, its release may aid an observer in identifying individuals when combined with other information, which is a privacy consideration. Implementors should take into account what other information they advertise through mechanisms such as Multicast DNS, how a Thing might otherwise be identified, and whether the Thing carries personal identifying information, and then apply appropriate data minimisation techniques.

Finally, the basic purpose of MUD is to configure access, so by its very nature it can be disruptive if used by unauthorized parties.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that can be asked for its own address can lie about it, so a MUD URL sent in the clear should not be trusted to grant extra access. The file is also a hint to an attacker about what the device is and what bugs it might have.

items.title: Not for general purpose computers
items.text: Their makers cannot describe a specific communication pattern, so there is nothing for the network to enforce.

items.title: Not a substitute for patching
items.text: MUD can reduce exposure when a vulnerability exists, but it never replaces the need for manufacturers to patch.

items.title: Not a directive
items.text: What the manufacturer specifies is a suggestion. How it is applied locally is up to the network administrator.
